newsitem.title: UK: Concerns mount as rebels stunt Colombia GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Concerns mount as rebels stunt Colombia GDP growth.

text.p: Investors are weighing the cost of a resurgence of guerrilla violence in Colombia and are keeping an eye on trouble spots elsewhere in Latin America for fear that rebel activity will become a serious drag on growth.
Investors are concerned about how far Bogota is diverting funds out of infrastructure and into defence as it fights a rear-guard action against drug lords and left-wing guerrillas.

"We are watching very carefully the development of the (Colombian) government's battle with the guerrillas, which is causing a diversion of government spending from infrastructure to security," said Joe MacHatton, Latin America strategist at Kleinwort Benson in London.

"It has caused a slowdown in GDP growth," he said. "In 1995, GDP grew at 5.2 percent and in 1996, we are looking for 3.0 percent. We had expected 3.5 percent for 1997, but if problems continue at this rate, it could be closer to 3.0 percent."
Analysts at Merrill Lynch are more bullish, looking for 3.0 to 3.5 percent GDP growth this year and at least 4.0 in 1997.
But they concede that political turbulence, which has given the guerrillas an opportunity to wreak havoc, is partly weighing on this year's GDP numbers.
For the past year, Colombia's President Ernesto Samper has been dogged by allegations his 1994 election campaign was bankrolled by drug barons and has been under pressure to quit.
Key political figures have resigned, and the rebels have taken advantage of the government's distraction to escalate their campaign.
Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol estimated this week that rebel attacks on its main pipeline between January and September had cost it $38 million in lost production and clean-up work.
But Merrill Lynch said the impact of rebel attacks was cushioned by rising oil prices, arguing that every $1 increase meant a $120-million rise in Colombia's export earnings.
"The increase in oil prices more than offsets the impact of of temporary shutdowns of the pipeline," it said.

While most Latin American countries are now slashing their defence budgets, Bogota has called for a sharp rise in defence spending for 1997 and hopes to raise $420 million by obliging rich individuals and firms to buy five-year "war bonds."
Economists say such defence spending will divert funds from crucial infrastructure projects, including the rebuilding of Colombia's crumbling road network.
A resurgence in kidnappings, in a country that already counts the highest rate of abductions in the world, is also sapping funds that would otherwise go into the economy.

"The guerrillas, in escalating their war against the government, have taken on other revenue earners like kidnapping -- resulting in five to six abductions per day and millions of dollars in ransom payments," Kleinwort's MacHatton said. "This is stopping money going into the system."

While Colombia's situation echoes Peru's prolonged battle against Shining Path guerrillas, investors say the 1992 arrest of rebel leader Abimael Guzman was a turning point in Peru and that things have improved enormously there since then.

Mexico's Chiappas rebellion also took a heavy toll on its markets last year. However, the emergence four months ago of a new rebel group there has caused scarcely a ripple because its activities have been mostly confined to rural districts so far.

But "It would create enormous anxiety among the population and among foreign investors if (the rebellion) moves into the urban areas," said Ondine Smulders, Latin America strategist at HSBC James Capel, adding both direct and portfolio investment would suffer heavily. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
